walkthroughs.body_html:
Understanding Business Activity — a core area of GCSE Business Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Understanding Business Activity brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Understanding Business Activity.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Porter
Friedman
Carroll

mcqs.q: What did Mayo's Hawthorne studies suggest about motivation?
options: Mayo proved that better lighting increases productivity.
Mayo invented the assembly line.
Liquidity ratios measure how quickly a business sells products.

Workers are motivated by social factors and the feeling of being noticed/valued — not just pay or physical conditions. Productivity rose because researchers paid attention to workers, not because lighting improved.

mcqs.q: What does a liquidity ratio like the current ratio measure?
options: Mayo invented the assembly line.
Liquidity ratios measure how quickly a business sells products.
A business's ability to meet short-term obligations — current assets divided by current liabilities. A ratio above 1 means assets cover liabilities; too high may indicate poor use of resources.
A higher liquidity ratio is always better.

mcqs.q: Why are cash flow and profit different on different time-scales?
options: Mayo invented the assembly line.
Cash flow and profit are the same thing measured differently.

Profit is recognised when a sale is made (even on credit); cash flow is when money actually moves. A profitable sale today may produce no cash for 60 days while bills are due — creating a cash-flow problem despite profit.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.
